Long ago, when the world was young, the Sky Fox roamed the heavens with a coat of pure silver. She was lonely, for she was the only creature who could leap between the stars.

One winter night, the Sky Fox gazed down at Earth and saw people huddled in darkness, shivering through the endless polar night. Her heart ached for them. She wanted to bring them light, but the sun had traveled far to the south.

From that night forward, whenever the darkness grows too heavy, the Sky Fox runs across the Arctic sky. Her tail paints rivers of color across the darkness, reminding all who see them that even in the deepest cold and longest night, there is beauty, magic, and hope.

The people call her gift the Northern Lights.

**The Weaver of Dawn**

In the time before time, darkness covered the world like a thick blanket. The people huddled in caves, knowing nothing of color or warmth.

High in the mountains lived an old weaver named Alara. Each night, she worked at her loom, though she could not see the threads she wove. Her fingers moved by memory alone, creating patterns she had never witnessed.

One night, a silver spider descended from the ceiling. "Why do you weave in darkness?" it asked.

"Because I have faith," Alara replied, "that my work has purpose, even unseen."

The spider was moved by her trust. "I will give you a gift," it said, and from its spinnerets came a single golden thread that glowed with inner light.

Alara wove this thread into her tapestry. As she worked, the thread multiplied, spreading light across her creation. The warmth grew until the entire tapestry blazed brilliant. She carried it outside and hung it in the sky.

That tapestry became the sun, and its light revealed all the beautiful patterns Alara had woven in darkness—now visible as the first sunrise.

The people learned that faith and patient work, even when unseen, can illuminate the world.

A mirror named Lyra grew weary of her own reflection. She tilted herself toward the void, allowing her surface to catch something beyond—the faint glimmer of another mirror in the distance. In doing so, she reflected not herself but another's light.

A mirror named Orion received Lyra's reflection and, moved by this gift, angled himself to reflect her back, adding his own luminescence to what he returned.

Other mirrors witnessed this exchange. A bronze mirror offered warmth. A silver mirror contributed clarity. A crystal mirror gave depth. Each turned away from their own reflection to catch and return the light of others.

As more mirrors joined, the reflections multiplied infinitely—each mirror now showing not one image but thousands, each containing all the others. The void between them filled with cascading light, and they realized their individual surfaces had always been fragments of one great mirror.

Now they understand: we see ourselves most truly not in our own reflection, but in the light we exchange. In turning toward each other, we become whole.
